method: Topic and fact notes written from a pre-2022 or 2023 human article; each model writes an article of matched length from the notes alone, so the human wording never reaches it (Graphite 2026 design). The notes are terse fact fragments with no evaluative wording, so they carry no style into the output.

items.topic: a museum field-trip activity on globalization for school classes
notes: museum-wide activity: student teams gather data on everyday things they use
guiding question: what would life be like if you could only buy foods native to New York State
three teams, each with a chaperone or teacher: foods (Super Kids Market), fashions (museum collections), fads (TimeLab)
each team makes a chart of its findings and leads a short discussion on global interdependence
before the visit: post North, South, East, West on classroom walls; each student writes a US state on a card and stands where it would be; repeat with continents, oceans, countries
one-week 'globalization journal': imported cheese, imported CDs, a TV show made abroad, news about international business
classroom world map where students pin objects and images from other countries; weekly discussion

items.topic: how the calendar shapes the birds seen in Ohio through the year
notes: 'almanac' comes from Arabic al-manakh (calendar, earlier weather); possibly from a place where camels kneel, a seasonal camp
Ohio sits between the Mississippi and Atlantic flyways, at the edge of prairie and forest
latitude governs timing: migration, daylight length, breeding; glaciers shaped Lake Erie, the Ohio River, plains and hills
breeding success depends on timing: arriving early risks too little food; a second brood risks food running out
over about 200 years humans removed predators, warmed the climate, introduced exotic species, destroyed habitat
50 or more species are present year-round, but crows, robins, blue jays and song sparrows are partly migratory, so the individuals change
robins eat worms alone in summer, flock to eat fruit in winter
range expansions: mockingbirds, titmice, cardinals, house finches; lost from Ohio: prairie-chickens, Bachman's sparrow, Bewick's wren
extinct: passenger pigeon, Eskimo curlew, Carolina parakeet
analogs of the trigonometric functions: sinh, cosh, tanh and their inverses (arsinh etc.)
points (cos t, sin t) trace a unit circle; points (cosh t, sinh t) trace the right half of the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1
introduced in the 18th century by Johann Heinrich Lambert
appear in solutions of the catenary equation and Laplace's equation (electromagnetism, heat transfer, fluid dynamics, special relativity)
identity cosh^2 x - sinh^2 x = 1
derivative of sinh is cosh and of cosh is sinh (no sign change, unlike cos)
cosh is even, sinh is odd, sinh 0 = 0, cosh t >= 1
Osborn's rule converts trigonometric identities to hyperbolic ones by flipping signs on some product terms
the curve a cosh(x/a) is the catenary, the shape of a hanging chain
periodic with complex period 2*pi*i; defined from exponentials, e.g. sinh x = (e^x - e^-x)/2

items.topic: a study finding that black holes in small galaxies are smaller than expected
notes: Nicholas Scott and Alister Graham, Swinburne University of Technology, Melbourne
database of 77 galaxies and their central black holes, data from Chile, Hawaii and the Hubble Space Telescope
black hole mass measured from how fast stars orbit it
older theory: fixed ratio of galaxy mass to black hole mass; it held for large galaxies only
finding: each ten-fold drop in galaxy mass gives a hundred-fold drop in black hole mass
small galaxies have denser central star populations, so their black holes grow faster
when large galaxies merge the black holes double; when small ones merge they quadruple
possible answer to the missing intermediate-mass black holes (10,000 to a few hundred thousand solar masses)
paper to appear in the Astrophysical Journal; next-generation large telescopes may see them directly
stars appear to rise and set because the Earth rotates
this apparent motion led early thinkers to an Earth-centered universe; Copernicus corrected it
a sidereal day is just under 24 hours, one rotation relative to the stars
differs from solar time (based on the Sun) and lunar cycles (about 28 days)
defined from the hour angle of the vernal equinox
the equator and the prime meridian at Greenwich are the zero lines of latitude and longitude
at the equinoxes day and night are each 12 hours
astronomers use sidereal time to predict star positions; values are tabulated in an ephemeris
the U.S. Naval Observatory offers an online sidereal-time clock

items.topic: restoring longleaf pine forests in Mississippi
notes: longleaf pines survived Hurricane Katrina 48 percent better than loblolly pines
longleaf forests once covered 90 million acres in the South; now about 3 million
gopher tortoise is a keystone species; more than 300 species use its burrows
at least 122 endangered or threatened species; up to 300 groundcover plant species per acre
landowner Orby Wright, Purvis, Mississippi, bought about 2,000 acres (Quail Hollow Ranch) from a pecan company
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Healthy Forests Reserve Program, part of the nine-state Longleaf Pine Initiative
the ecosystem needs periodic fire; Wright installed fire lanes and does prescribed burns
NRCS has helped restore 1,641 acres and burn 1,812 acres in Mississippi; 669 acres restored in Lamar County in 2010
participants get money for planting, firebreaks, prescribed burning, invasive-plant control

items.topic: a Caltech experiment raising an obelisk with a kite
notes: team led by Gharib at Caltech, with Graff and Clemmons
raised a four-ton concrete obelisk using a kite and a pulley system
plan to replace steel scaffolding and pulleys with wooden ones, and later windlasses like those on Egyptian ships
the obelisk base drags a few feet as it rises, which keeps it from swinging past vertical
a couple of workers guide the operation with ropes
no evidence that Egyptians used kites; a frieze in a Cairo museum shows an unusual wing pattern above men near what may be ropes
Gharib: 'We're not Egyptologists'; the aim is to test whether the method is possible
next tests: a ten-ton stone; hope to try an obelisk still lying in an Egyptian quarry; a drag chute might replace the kite
steady winds up to 30 mph are common near the pyramid and obelisk sites

items.topic: how wind shear helps produce tornadoes
notes: wind shear is the change in wind speed and direction with height
most strong tornadoes come from supercell thunderstorms
thunderstorms are driven by an updraft of rising air
shear makes a horizontal rolling column of air
rain-cooled air is heavier and forms a downdraft
the updraft tilts the horizontal spinning column to vertical
the result is a rotating thunderstorm that can produce a tornado

items.topic: the Japanese community in Melbourne, Australia
notes: includes expatriates, temporary residents and Japanese Australians
as of 2007 many lived in suburbs such as Brighton and Camberwell; young people in Prahran; single corporate employees in Toorak
Camberwell North: 110 Japan-born residents in 1996, 116 in 2001
families settled around Caulfield after the Japanese School of Melbourne opened on 13 May 1986
institutions: Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (1963), Japanese Society of Melbourne (1965), Japan Club of Victoria, Consulate-General
Saturday Japanese program from September 1972; supplementary school at Oakleigh South Primary School from 1986
in 1996, 400 children aged 6-15; about 75% attended Australian schools
Japan Festival in the City of Whitehorse; over 300 people at an athletics event in Fawkner Park on 26 October 1997 (Tetsuo Mizukami)

items.topic: North Mountain, a wildland in western Virginia
notes: in the George Washington and Jefferson National Forests; part of the Craig Creek Cluster
Wilderness Society calls it a 'Mountain Treasure'
about 6 miles southeast of New Castle, Virginia, between VA 779 and Forest Road 224
North Mountain Trail (Forest Trail 263, 13.2 miles, yellow blazes); Deer, Turkey and Grouse trails about 1.5 miles each
old logging roads from early 20th-century timbering are still passable
forest of oaks, hickory, poplar, hemlock; table mountain pine needs fire because its cones open with heat
rare species: pirate bush, small spreading pogonia, sword-leaved phlox, orangefin madtom
elevation from 1,410 feet to 3,062 feet; about 75 percent underlain by Silurian sandstone
inventoried roadless area, protected from road building and timber sales
herbicide used on Tree of Heaven along Forest Road 224; 1998 Broad Run sale of 42 acres done as public firewood cutting
in Trainer, Delaware County, on the Delaware River, 15 miles southwest of Philadelphia
owned since June 2012 by Monroe Energy, a subsidiary of Delta Air Lines
produces jet fuel, gasoline, diesel and home heating oil
1891: Union Petroleum leased 17 acres; the wooden plant burned in 1912
Sinclair Oil opened a $7 million plant on 17 March 1925
1955: new crude stills, about 120,000 barrels per day
later owners: Atlantic Richfield (1969), BP/SOHIO, Tosco (1996), Phillips, ConocoPhillips; shut in September 2011
Delta bought it in 2012 and spent about $100 million to shift 40% of output to jet fuel; capacity 185,000 barrels per day
2014: five-year deal with Bridger LLC for 65,000 barrels per day of domestic crude

items.topic: the blues song "You've Got to Love Her with a Feeling"
notes: first recorded by Tampa Red in 1938 as "Love with a Feeling", a mid-tempo twelve-bar blues
Tampa Red on vocal and slide guitar, Black Bob Hudson on piano
Tampa Red recut it in May 1950 in Chicago style, and solo in 1961
Freddie King recorded it in Cincinnati on 26 August 1960 with stop-time breaks
released as a B-side on Federal Records; reached number 93 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1961, his first chart single
Junior Wells recorded it on On Tap (1974) and live at Buddy Guy's Legends in November 1996
many blues artists covered it, making it a blues standard

items.topic: the Knorr Hut in the Wetterstein Mountains
notes: mountain hut of the German Alpine Club's Munich Section, at 2,052 m
on the edge of the Zugspitzplatt, on the normal route from Garmisch-Partenkirchen to the Zugspitze
first built by 1855 as a small refuge, funded partly by merchant Angelo Knorr
run down by 1860; rebuilt and opened on 10 August 1873 for 20 to 25 people
approach from Garmisch-Partenkirchen through the Partnach Gorge and Reintal valley, 6 to 7 hours
approach from Ehrwald via the Ehrwalder Alm and the Gatterl, about 2.5 hours
base for the Jubilee Ridge to the Zugspitze, joined at about 2,650 m

items.topic: Sally Stevens, a session singer and vocal contractor
notes: born 24 November 1939 in Los Angeles; studied music at UCLA
sings the main title of The Simpsons and of Family Guy
vocal contractor and singer for hundreds of films, including Forrest Gump, The Abyss and Amistad
first film scoring work in 1962 on How the West Was Won; later Doctor Zhivago and The Sound of Music
production singer in Las Vegas 1961-62; TV variety shows including The Carol Burnett Show
recorded with Frank Sinatra, Andy Williams, Neil Diamond and others
lead vocal on "Tomorrow's Child" at EPCOT's Spaceship Earth, 1986-1994
choral director of the Oscars broadcasts for over 20 years, through 2018
co-wrote "Who Comes This Night" with Dave Grusin, recorded by James Taylor in 2005
also publishes short fiction and poetry and exhibits black-and-white photography; long service on AFTRA and SAG boards

items.topic: The First Letter, a 1991 album by Wire
notes: ninth studio album, released October 1991 on Mute Records, credited to "Wir"
the band became Wir after drummer Robert Gotobed left over the use of drum machines
the band then went on hiatus until 1999 and released new material again in 2002
single: "So and Slow It Grows"
"Take It (For Greedy)" is built from samples of Wire's own 1970s records; Colin Newman found that funny
Gotobed appears in sampled form through a snare drum taken from an old album
Bruce Gilbert sings lead on "Ticking Mouth"
Stereogum ranked it 11th of 15 Wire albums; Trouser Press called it livelier than A Bell Is a Cup; AllMusic said the textures matter more than the songs
produced by Wir and Paul Kendall

items.topic: Sergey Lugansky, a Soviet fighter pilot
notes: born 1 October 1918 in Verniy (now Almaty, Kazakhstan); died 16 January 1977
graduated Orenburg Military Aviation School in December 1938
flew 59 sorties on the I-153 in the Winter War, 1939-40
at the front from October 1941; flew LaGG-3, then Yak-1 from 1943
the city of Alma-Ata paid for a custom-painted Yak-1 for him
1944: mock dogfight with a visiting American colonel flying a P-63
commanded the regiment from June 1944, renamed 152nd Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment
390 sorties and at least 34 solo victories; twice Hero of the Soviet Union (2 September 1943, 1 July 1944)
after the war commanded fighter divisions flying MiG-15 and MiG-17; General-Major of Aviation in 1957; retired December 1964
a 1968 stroke left him partly paralyzed; friend of fellow ace Talgat Bigeldinov
